newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Jobless drop shows Portugal economy buoyant.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Jobless drop shows Portugal economy buoyant.

text.p: The biggest drop in unemployment for four years sent a strong signal on Thursday of the increasing health of the Portuguese economy, analysts said.
According to the Employment Ministry, the number of people registered as jobless fell to 435,048 in June, a 6.5 percent drop on the same month last year and the largest such decline since 1993.
The ministry said that the strongest fall had been seen amongst the young, where the numbers out of work slid nearly 20 percent to 99,000 compared with the same 1996 month.
"This proves that the strategy applied by the government in fighting unemployment has begun to produce significant results," the ministry proclaimed in a statement accompanying the figures.
The figures were the latest indication that the Portuguese economy has been expanding faster in the past few months than the government had predicted when it drew up its budget plans.
Officially, the government is still sticking to its 2.75-3.25 percent target but the Bank of Portugal has already raised its forecast to 3.0-3.75 percent for 1997.
The economy, as measured by gross domestic product (GDP), grew at least three percent in 1996.

"If there is going to be any revision, then clearly it is going to be upwards," said one government economist who asked not to be named. "Things are obviously much better than in October when the (budget) plan was drawn up," he added.
But the official said that a formal revision of the government numbers would probably have to wait until after the summer when all the data for the first half of the year would be available.

One consequence of the faster growth is that the Socialist administration of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres should face few problems in meeting its budget target for 1997 which crucial to its chances of securing a place for Portugal in the European Union's planned single currency, analysts said.
Two of the biggest contributors to the stronger than anticipated economic growth have been the construction sector and tourism, officials said.

The former has been boosted by the approach of the 1998 World Fair in Lisbon, although there are also clear signs of increased activity in the private construction sector. Tourism has been helped by the strength of the British pound and the dollar which make Portuguese holidays cheaper.

Exports, however, which many analysts expected to be a motor of growth, are sending mixed signals perhaps because of distortions created by a truck strike in Spain earlier this year, the officials added.
But despite the strong growth and falling unemployment, economists and government officials say that there are no signs of inflationary tension either from goods or wages.

Salomon Brothers economist Jose Luis Alzola said that it would probably need 12 to 18 months of growth at around four percent to take up all the slack in the economy and start producing supply pressure.
"There are no signs yet on the pay side," said the government economist.

In part the lack of wage pressure was due to the fact that manufacturing industry was still shedding labour with the recent growth in employment being registered largely in the agricultural sector, he added.
"If we can maintain a level of moderate wage growth, then we should be able to ensure that the economy stays competitive," the economist said.
